answer:
FULL ANALYSIS COMPLETE — hypothesis answering "Does increased time preference lead to higher BMI?"

NATURAL-LANGUAGE HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, associational wording)
In the NLSY79 cohort (12,686 respondents; analysis samples n≈3,500–6,300), higher time preference — operationalized as present-oriented financial behavior: taking more money out of savings than putting in (dissaving), lower net savings flows, and lower accumulated wealth — is associated with modestly HIGHER BMI. Respondents who dissaved in 1989 had on average ~0.26 BMI units higher BMI in 1989 than all others (b=+0.262, SE=0.130, p=0.044), rising to +0.45 (SE=0.136, p=0.001) once the "no savings" group is modeled separately ("no savings" is itself the highest-BMI group, +0.54, SE=0.158, p=0.0007 — it is NOT pooled with savers). Each quintile increase in net savings flow is associated with −0.19 BMI units (SE=0.050, p=0.0002), i.e., the most patient quintile carries ~0.75 BMI units less than the least patient. Dissaving also predicts BMI GAIN between 1981 and 1989 (+0.196 BMI units, SE=0.089, p=0.028), and the obesity-logit odds ratio for dissaving is 1.17 (p=0.058). Wealth-based measures are weaker: wealth growth 1985→1990 is null (b=−0.003, p=0.71), while 1996 wealth level is protective (b=−0.030 sign-log units, SE=0.013, p=0.021). The association is partially mediated/confounded by contemporaneous income — adding 1989 income attenuates the dissaving coefficient from +0.26 to +0.17 (p=0.23). Bottom line: the data support a positive association between present-oriented (impatient) financial behavior and BMI, of small-to-moderate magnitude (~0.2–0.5 BMI units; roughly 0.6–1.5 kg at median height), with the caveat that "leads to" cannot be established causally — reverse causality (poor health/BMI driving financial strain) and unmeasured confounding (e.g., self-control) are plausible; wealth-accumulation measures provide only weak corroboration.

KEY RESULTS (OLS, HC1 robust; outcome BMI 1989 from Weight 1989 × Height 1985; covariates: sex, race, age 1979, family size, mother's/father's/own education, ASVAB, log 1979 income, ever-institutionalized)
- A1 dissaved vs rest: b=+0.262, SE=0.130, p=0.044, 95% CI [0.007, 0.518], n=6,295
- A2 4-level (ref=saved/no change): dissaved b=+0.447, SE=0.136, p=0.001; no-savings b=+0.536, SE=0.158, p=0.0007, n=6,295
- A3 net savings flow (per $10k, winsorized): b=−0.201, SE=0.123, p=0.103, n=3,481
- A4 net flow quintiles: b=−0.186 per quintile, SE=0.050, p=0.0002, n=3,481
- A5 wealth growth 1985→1990: b=−0.003, SE=0.009, p=0.71, n=5,244
- A6 log wealth 1996: b=−0.030, SE=0.013, p=0.021, n=4,245
Secondary: dissaving → BMI1992 b=+0.273 (p=0.080, n=5,253); dissaving → ΔBMI 1981→1989 b=+0.196 (p=0.028, n=6,224); wealth growth → ΔBMI b=−0.002 (p=0.71, n=5,196). Robustness: obesity logit OR=1.171 (p=0.058, n=6,295). Sensitivity: +1989 income → dissaving b=+0.166 (p=0.23, n=5,296); covariate median/missing-indicator imputation → dissaving b=+0.155 (p=0.13, n=10,153), wealth growth b=−0.003 (p=0.71, n=8,318).

COMPLETE-CASE N PER SPEC AND ATTRITION/BALANCE
- BMI-1989 base sample n=10,179 (BMI mean 25.01, SD 4.72); savings-direction spec n=6,295; net-flow spec n=3,481 (amounts asked only of savers/dissavers, mutually exclusive); wealth-growth spec n=5,244; wealth-1996 spec n=4,245. Imputed-covariate versions: n=10,153 (savings) and n=8,318 (wealth growth).
- Covariate balance across specs is close: % male 48.9–51.1, % Black 16.4–18.8, mean age 1979 17.5–17.6, mean education 10.4, mean log-income 9.35–9.47 — the shrinking wealth samples are slightly more male/Black/higher-income but not dramatically selected; still, the wealth-spec nulls could reflect reduced power and selection rather than a true absence of association.

WORKFLOW (executed; script nls_bmi_analysis.py, coefficient table nls_bmi_results.csv)
1. Load and validate 12,686×61 CSV against schema (names match 1:1; unit corrections: weights lb→kg ×0.45359237; Height 1981 decoded from feet-inches concatenation FII→inches, e.g., 507=67"; Height 1985 used as the adult height in the primary spec).
2. Cleaning: weight sentinel 996 (11 obs) and implausible ranges → missing; BMI winsorized to plausible 15–60; savings amounts ≥$1M (30 obs) treated as sentinel; net flow = put − took (mutually exclusive fields combined), winsorized at 1st/99th pct; wealth transformed sign(x)·log1p(|x|) to handle negative net worth; income top-codes retained but log1p-transformed; education sentinel 95 dropped; ever-institutionalized = residence code 5 (Jail) in any wave 1981–1996 OR sentenced before 1980.
3. Exposures (reported separately, never pooled blindly): dissaving indicator (code 2), 4-level savings direction with "no savings" (code 4) as its own term, net savings flow (continuous + quintiles), wealth growth 1985→1990, wealth level 1996.
4. Models: OLS with HC1 robust SEs for BMI level and BMI change (1981→1989); logistic for obesity (BMI≥30); all specs adjusted for the covariate set above; contemporaneous 1989 income shown only as sensitivity (collider concern); missing-data sensitivity via median + missing-indicator imputation of covariates (outcome/exposure kept complete-case).

ASSUMPTIONS CARRIED FORWARD
- Weights are pounds and Height 1981 is a feet-inches encoding (schema labels are wrong); Height 1985 is inches.
- Savings amounts are nominal dollars; sentinels/top-codes represent invalid/capped values.
- Savings/wealth behavior is a noisy proxy for time preference; the analysis is associational.
- No pregnancy flag exists, so some female BMI values may reflect pregnancy (unfixable with available columns).
- "No savings" (code 4) reported separately because it may mix inability and choice not to save.

UNCERTAINTIES/LIMITATIONS
- Causal direction unknown; contemporaneous income absorbs much of the dissaving–BMI association (attenuation from p=0.044/p=0.001 to p=0.23), so part of the raw association is socioeconomic.
- Wealth-based exposures shrink the sample by 40–60% (attrition) and are top-coded; their near-null results may reflect reduced power and selection rather than a true absence of association.
- Timing misalignment: 1989 savings flow is measured "since last interview," while BMI is point-in-time.
- Effect sizes are modest relative to BMI SD (~4.7), and imputation sensitivity weakens significance of the dissaving coefficient (b=+0.155, p=0.13), so the strongest defensible claim is a consistent small positive association, strongest for the savings-flow measures, weakest for wealth accumulation.

payload.hypothesis: In NLSY79, higher time preference (present-oriented financial behavior: dissaving, lower net savings flow, lower accumulated wealth) is associated with modestly higher BMI: dissavers in 1989 had ~0.26 BMI units higher BMI in 1989 (+0.45 vs savers when 'no savings' is modeled separately; 'no savings' group +0.54), each savings-flow quintile of higher saving is associated with -0.19 BMI units, and dissaving predicts BMI gain 1981-1989 (+0.20, p=0.028); obesity odds ratio 1.17 (p=0.058). Wealth accumulation 1985-1990 shows no association (p=0.71) while 1996 wealth level is weakly protective (-0.030, p=0.021). Contemporaneous income accounts for part of the association (coefficient attenuates to +0.17, p=0.23). The association is consistent in direction but modest (~0.2-0.5 BMI units); causality cannot be established from these observational data, and reverse causality is plausible.
payload.workflow: Validated 12,686x61 NLSY79 extract against schema; corrected units (weights lb->kg; Height 1981 decoded from feet-inches concatenation, Height 1985 used as adult height); recoded sentinels (weight 996, savings amounts >=1e6, grade 95, wealth/income top-codes); constructed BMI 1981/1989/1992 (plausible range 15-60); built time-preference exposures (dissaving indicator, 4-level savings direction with 'no savings' separate, winsorized/quintiled net savings flow, sign-log wealth growth 1985->1990, wealth level 1996); HC1-robust OLS of BMI 1989 and BMI change 1981->1989 and obesity logit adjusted for sex, race cohort, age, family size, parental and own education, ASVAB, log 1979 income, and an ever-institutionalized indicator; sensitivities: contemporaneous 1989 income (collider check), median+missing-indicator imputation of covariates, quintile exposures; complete-case n reported per spec (6,295 savings-direction; 3,481 net-flow; 5,244 wealth-growth; 4,245 wealth-1996) with covariate-balance/attrition diagnostics across specs.
